Ice, liquid water, and steam are all water. So what makes them so different?
matter. Anything that takes up space. Your desk, your juice, and the air are all matter.
solid. Matter that keeps its own shape. A rock and an ice cube are solids.
liquid. Matter that flows and takes the shape of its container. Milk and water are liquids.
gas. Matter that spreads out to fill all the space it is in. The air you breathe is a gas.
melting. When a solid heats up and turns into a liquid. An ice pop melting in the sun is melting.
freezing. When a liquid cools down and turns into a solid. Water in a freezer freezes into ice.
condensation. When a gas cools down and turns into a liquid. Drops on a cold glass of lemonade are condensation.

Matter is anything that takes up space. Matter comes in three main states . A solid keeps its own shape. A liquid flows and takes the shape of its cup. A gas spreads out to fill all the space it is in.

I want to sort a block, juice, and air. First I ask: does it keep its shape? The block does, so it is a solid. Does it flow and take the shape of its cup? Juice does, so it is a liquid. Does it spread out everywhere? Air does, so it is a gas.

Pour milk from a tall glass into a flat bowl. Did the milk change shape? Yes. It took the shape of the bowl. Did the amount of milk change? No. So milk is a liquid . Now put a toy block in the bowl. It stays a cube. The block is a solid .

Heating can change matter from one state to another. When ice warms up, it melts into liquid water. Water melts and freezes at 32°F . When liquid water gets hot, it turns into a gas called water vapor . At 212°F , water boils and turns to vapor fast.
I leave a chocolate bar in a hot car. Later it is soft and runny. Why? The heat made the solid chocolate melt. It turned into a liquid. The chocolate is still chocolate. Only its state changed.

A pot of water sits on a hot stove. Small bubbles appear. Then big bubbles roll up fast. What is in the big bubbles? Water vapor , a gas. The heat turned liquid water into a gas. The water is boiling . If we waited long enough, the pot would boil dry.

Cooling changes matter too. When liquid water gets colder than 32°F, it freezes into ice. When water vapor cools, it turns back into liquid drops. This is condensation . Many changes can go back and forth. Some changes cannot be undone. A cooked egg cannot turn raw again!

On a hot day, I hold a glass of ice water. The outside of the glass gets wet. Did water leak through the glass? No, the glass has no holes. The air has water vapor in it. The cold glass cooled the vapor. It turned into tiny liquid drops. That is condensation.

Pour juice into an ice pop mold. Put it in the freezer. The next day it is hard. The juice froze . It went from liquid to solid. Now leave the pop in the sun. It melts back into juice. This change can go back , so it is not like cooking an egg.

Four ice cubes, all the same size, each in the same kind of small dish. Only the place was different. Sunny windowsill, 85 degrees: melted in 25 minutes. Kitchen counter, 72 degrees: melted in 50 minutes. Refrigerator, 38 degrees: melted in about 4 hours. Freezer, 0 degrees: did not melt. It was still ice the next day.

Alice Ball. A Black American chemist from Seattle, Washington. A chemist studies what things are made of and how they change. Oil from the seeds of the chaulmoogra tree could help people with Hansen's disease , a sickness of the skin and nerves. But the oil was thick and sticky. In Hawaiʻi, Alice Ball found a way to change the oil so doctors could give it as a shot. It helped many people. She died young, at 24. After she died, a man at her college took credit for her work. Today people know it was hers.

Frederick McKinley Jones. A Black American inventor from Cincinnati, Ohio. He was mostly self-taught . In the late 1930s, he designed a cooling machine for trucks . Now trucks could carry food and medicine far away without it spoiling. Cold food stayed cold. Frozen food stayed frozen!

Mary Engle Pennington. A chemist who studied how to keep food safe . She led a U.S. government food lab. Her work showed how keeping food cold helps it stay fresh and safe. She also studied railroad cars that kept food cold on long trips.

Ukichiro Nakaya. A Japanese scientist who studied snow . In 1936, he was the first person to grow a snow crystal in a lab . In a very cold room, water vapor froze onto a single rabbit hair. He found that a snowflake's shape depends on how cold and how wet the air is.
